questions.problem: Find the point of intersection of the lines $y=-3x+4$ and $y=3x-2.$
questions.worked_solution:
The point of intersection consists of the coordinates $(x,y)$ that satisfy both equations $y=-3x+4$ and $y=3x-2.$ So, we need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=-3x+4 \\ y=3x-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

We can solve this system by substitution. Substituting the first equation $y=-3x+4$ into the second equation $y=3x-2$ yields an equation that we can solve for $x:$   

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x+4 & =3x-2 \\ -6x & =-6 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is the $x$-coordinate of the point of intersection. To find the $y$-coordinate, we substitute $x=1$ back into one of the equations, say $y=3x-2,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3(1)-2 \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=1,\,y=1.$ So, the coordinates of the intersection point are  $(1,1).$

questions.problem: Find the point of intersection of the lines $y=4x+3$ and $y=-x-2.$
questions.worked_solution:
The point of intersection consists of the coordinates $(x,y)$ that satisfy both equations $y=4x+3$ and $y=-x-2.$ So, we need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=4x+3 \\ y=-x-2\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by substitution. Substituting the first equation $y=4x+3$ into the second equation $y=-x-2$ yields an equation that we can solve for $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+3 & =-x-2 \\ 5x & =-5 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

This is the $x$-coordinate of the point of intersection. To find the $y$-coordinate, we substitute $x=-1$ back into one of the equations, say $y=-x-2,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-x-2 \\  & =-(-1)-2 \\  & =1-2 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=-1$ and $y=-1.$ So, the coordinates of the intersection point are $(-1,-1).$

The point of intersection consists of the coordinates $(x,y)$ that satisfy both equations $y=3x-1$ and $y=-4x+6.$ So, we need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=3x-1 \\ y=-4x+6\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by substitution. Substituting the first equation $y=3x-1$ into the second equation $y=-4x+6$ yields an equation that we can solve for $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-1 & =-4x+6 \\ 3x & =-4x+7 \\ 7x & =7 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is the $x$-coordinate of the point of intersection. To find the $y$-coordinate, we substitute $x=1$ back into one of the equations, say $y=3x-1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x-1 \\  & =3(1)-1 \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=1,\,y=2.$ So, the coordinates of the intersection point are $(\,1,2\,).$

\begin{aligned}y & =5x+2 \\  & =5(-1)+2 \\  & =-5+2 \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=-1,\,y=-3.$ So, the coordinates of the intersection point are $(\,-1,-3\,).$

questions.worked_solution:
We need to solve the system of equations consisting of two lines:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x-y=6 \\ 2x+3y=2\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $3,$ then we will get a $-3y$ term that can cancel with the $3y$ in the second equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x-y=6 & |\,\times 3 \\ 2x+3y=2\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}3x-3y=18 \\ 2x+3y=2\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable and allows us to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-\cancel{3y} & =18 \\ 2x+\cancel{3y} & =2 \\ (3x+2x) & =(18+2) \\ 5x & =20 \\ x & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=4$ back into the equation $x-y=6$ to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y & =6 \\ 4-y & =6 \\ -y & =2 \\ y & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=4,\,y=-2.$ So the coordinates of the point of intersection are $(4,-2).$

questions.worked_solution:
We need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x+3y=5 \\ -x-6y=4\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $2,$ then we will get a $6y$ term that can cancel with the $-6y$ in the second equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x+3y=5 & |\,\times 2 \\ -x-6y=4 & \end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}8x+6y=10 \\ -x-6y=4\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable and allows us to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}8x+\cancel{6y} & =10 \\ -x-\cancel{6y} & =4 \\ (8x-x) & =(10+4) \\ 7x & =14 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=2$ into the equation $4x+3y=5$ to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+3y & =5 \\ 4(2)+3y & =5 \\ 8+3y & =5 \\ 3y & =-3 \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=2,\,y=-1.$ So the coordinates of the point of intersection are $(2,-1).$

We need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x-y=7 \\ 3x+2y=11\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $2,$ then we will get a $-2y$ term that can cancel with the $2y$ in the second equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x-y=7 & |\,\times 2 \\ 3x+2y=11 & \end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}2x-2y=14 \\ 3x+2y=11\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable and allows us to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-\cancel{2y} & =14 \\ 3x+\cancel{2y} & =11 \\ (2x+3x) & =(14+11) \\ 5x & =25 \\ x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=5$ into the equation $x-y=7$ to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y & =7 \\ 5-y & =7 \\ -y & =2 \\ y & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=5,\,y=-2.$ So the coordinates of the point of intersection are $(5,-2).$

Since $(-2,b)$ is the point of intersection of the two lines, the values $x=-2,\,y=b$ must solve the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x+y=a \\ 7x+2y=-2\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=-2,\,y=b$ to obtain a new system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4(-2)+b=a \\ 7(-2)+2b=-2\end{aligned}
$$

The system simplifies as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-8+b=a \\ b=6\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we know that $b=6.$ Then, we can substitute $b=6$ into the first equation and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-8+b & =a \\ -8+6 & =a \\ -2 & =a\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=-2$ and $b=6.$

\{\begin{aligned}y=-2x+2 \\ y=-5x-a\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=b,\,y=8$ to obtain a new system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}8=-2(b)+2 \\ 8=-5(b)-a\end{aligned}
$$

The system simplifies as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}8=-2b+2 \\ 8=-5b-a\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we know that $b=-3.$ Then, we can substitute $b=-3$ into the second equation and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =-5b-a \\ 8 & =-5(-3)-a \\ 8 & =15-a \\ -7 & =-a \\ 7 & =a\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=7$ and $b=-3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14220058/assets/e63b2ac5fe2bdfb905fe3c86706be4a556e5322698f9fd26ee115dba0a886f4b.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The point of intersection consists of the coordinates $(x,y)$ that satisfy both equations $y=5x+3$ and $y=x-1.$ So, we need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=5x+3 \\ y=x-1\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the substitution method to solve the system. Substituting the first equation $y=5x+3$ into the second equation $y=x-1$ gives an equation that we can solve for $x\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}5x+3 & =x-1 \\ 5x & =x-4 \\ 4x & =-4 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

This is the $x$-coordinate of the point of intersection. To find the $y$-coordinate, we substitute $x = -1$ back into one of the equations, say $y=x-1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x-1 \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=-1, \, y=-2.$ So, the coordinates of the intersection point are $(-1,-2).$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the point of intersection of the lines $x + 2 y = 1$ and $2 x - y = 7.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x+2y=1 \\ 2x-y=7\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the second equation by $2,$ then we will get a $-2y$ term that can cancel with the $2y$ term in the first equation:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14220058/assets/d2cac87bca62cf4fa8cc6ad3c0bd289de7cb0f8c39e742dd6e7731cb90b0e354.svg)

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable and allows us to solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\cancel{2y} & =1 \\ 4x-\cancel{2y} & =14 \\ (x+4x) & =(1+14) \\ 5x & =15 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=3$ into the equation $x+2y=1$ to solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2y & =1 \\ 3+2y & =1 \\ 2y & =-2 \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=3, \, y=-1.$ So the coordinates of the point of intersection are $(3,-1).$

Example: 
                    Calculating Unknown Parameters Given a Point of Intersection
canonical_examples.problem: The lines $y = -3 x + a$ and $y = x - 1$ intersect at the point $C$ with coordinates $(b, -4).$ Find the parameters $a$ and $b.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $(b,-4)$ is the point of intersection of the two lines, the values $x=b, \, y=-4$ must solve the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=-3x+a \\ y=x-1\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=b, \, y=-4$ to obtain a new system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4=-3b+a \\ -4=b-1\end{aligned}
$$

In the second equation, we can solve for $b\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =b-1 \\ -3 & =b\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can substitute $b=-3$ into the first equation and solve for $a\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =-3b+a \\ -4 & =-3(-3)+a \\ -4 & =9+a \\ -13 & =a\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a = -13$ and $b = -3.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we want to find the point of intersection between the two lines $y = x + 2$ and $y = 2x + 1.$ A sketch of both lines and the point of intersection $P$ is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14220058/assets/2bf429fdfbe706521b81617f56a0f561171aa7fd48e0af89318225f1d328e667.png)

The point $P$ consists of the coordinates $(x,y)$ that satisfy both equations $y=x+2$ and $y=2x+1.$ So, to find the coordinates of $P$ we need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=x+2 \\ y=2x+1\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by substitution. Substituting the first equation $y=x+2$ into the second equation $y=2x+1$ gives an equation that we can solve for $x\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =2x+1 \\ x+1 & =2x \\ 1 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

This is the $x$-coordinate of the point of intersection. To find the $y$-coordinate, we substitute $x = 1$ back into one of the equations, say $y=x+2,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x+2 \\  & =1+2 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=1, \, y=3.$ So, the point of intersection has the coordinates $(1,3).$
